item.title: CS 329Z: Agent Memory Architectures
item.description:
An assistant can give an excellent answer in one conversation, then ask you to explain your preferences, project, and completed work all over again in the next. It may reason well without connecting that ability to an ongoing history.

Agent memory addresses this discontinuity: turning past interactions into information that can be retrieved, updated, and used correctly in later actions.

The previous article, Context Management Patterns, examined what should enter each model call. This article asks what happens after information leaves the window: what gets stored, when it is written and retrieved, and how to establish whether memory improves later tasks.

This article follows Stanford CS 329Z Lecture 7: Agent Memory Architectures, moving from motivation and memory types through architectures, evaluation, and open problems. Engineering examples and implementation suggestions are my additions; experimental claims refer to their stated setups.

item.title: CS 329Z: Context Management Patterns
item.description:
A coding agent usually begins a bug fix with a clear objective: find the cause, change the code, and run tests. Dozens of turns later, its context may be full of search results, file fragments, terminal logs, and abandoned approaches. The user’s original constraints still exist somewhere in history, but the next decision may no longer use them correctly.

Long tasks require information to accumulate and to be reorganized. Context management decides what enters each model call, what stays in external storage, and what can temporarily be hidden.

Stanford CS 329Z Lecture 6 identifies five patterns:

1
2
3
4
5

Persistent event log   Store events and reconstruct model inputs
Memory offloading     Move knowledge into memory or files
Compaction            Replace longer histories with summaries
Observation masking   Hide old tool outputs, retain action structure
Context isolation     Give subtasks their own context

This article explains each pattern through the same bug-fixing example. The lecture’s context management section supplies the main framework; the handoff template, combined pipeline, and evaluation suggestions are my engineering synthesis.

item.title: Anthropic Agent Evolution II: Context Reset and Structured Handoff
item.description:
The central tension in long-running work is not whether a model can write code. It is that a task may last hours or days while every context window is finite. Replaying the entire history eventually creates both capacity and noise problems.

Anthropic’s first long-running agent harness answered with a simple principle: reset conversational context, but externalize project state into structured artifacts that the next agent can recover.

item.title: LangChain Agent Builder’s Memory System
item.description:
A meeting assistant writes paragraphs. You ask for lists instead. At the next meeting, it follows that preference without another reminder.

This kind of memory changes how an agent works, not merely what it can recall. Agent Builder represents instructions, capabilities, and knowledge as files so feedback can become rules available to future runs.
